Charting the Ocean Tracks

The tracks across the North Atlantic are drawn again twice a day, following the jet stream.[1] A flight eastbound rides the wind, and a flight westbound avoids it.

The planners publish the tracks as a short message that every crew reads before departure. See the crossing below, or the official track message for today.

Weather moves the tracks north or south by hundreds of miles from one day to the next, and the oceanic clearance names the track a crew may fly.

Shanwick and Gander share the ocean between them, handing each flight across at thirty degrees west.

Older charts show the tracks as fixed lines, but they have floated with the wind since the nineteen sixties.

The crossing

Once on the track, a crew reports at each waypoint and keeps the speed it was cleared for, so the tracks stay evenly spaced.

The jet stream again decides how long the crossing takes, sometimes by an hour or more.
